Unprecedented Heatwave Strikes France
France experienced at least 817 excess deaths between late July and August due to extreme heat, according to the national health agency. Since June, nearly 8,000 excess deaths have been recorded as a result of ongoing heatwaves, highlighting the impact of climate-induced temperature rises.
France is grappling with the deadly effects of heatwaves as the national health agency reported at least 817 excess deaths between July 27 and August 20 due to severe temperatures.
This spike contributes to a nearly 8,000 excess death toll since June, marking an alarming trend in climate change impacts.
Experts are urging immediate action to mitigate the health risks associated with rising temperatures, emphasizing the urgency of addressing global warming.

A mild heatwave is sweeping over different parts of the country.
"A mild heatwave is sweeping over Mymensingh and Sylhet divisions and the districts of Dhaka, Tangail, Manikgonj, Kishoregonj, Rajshahi, Sirajgonj, Rangpur, Nilphamari, Chandpur, Feni, Jashore, Chuadanga, Kushtia, Satkhira, Khulna, Barishal & Patuakhali, and it may abate in some places," said a Met Office bulletin issued this morning.
Besides, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) forecast rain in different parts of the country over the next 24 hours, starting at 9am.
"Light to moderate rain/thunder showers accompanied by temporary gusty winds are likely to occur at many places over Rangpur, Rajshahi, Mymensingh, Chattogram & Sylhet divisions and at a few places over Dhaka, Khulna & Barishal divisions," the bulletin said.
It also said moderately heavy falls may occur at places over Rangpur, Rajshahi, Mymensingh, Chattogram and Sylhet divisions.
Day and night temperatures may fall slightly over the country.
The highest temperature yesterday was 37.5 degrees Celsius in Feni, while today's minimum temperature is 24 degrees Celsius in Bandarban.
In the last 24 hours (till 6am today), the highest rainfall of 42 millimetres occurred in Bandarban.
The sun sets at 6:01pm today and rises at 5:45am tomorrow (17 September) in Dhaka.

Brutal heatwaves that persist through the night follow a hidden pattern
Heatwaves that persist through the night follow a hidden 10-to-30-day rhythm that could help forecasters spot dangerous heat earlier.
Some heatwaves let up after dark. You sweat through the afternoon, but by midnight there’s at least some relief.
Others don’t do that. The heat just carries straight through the night into the next scorching day, with no real chance to recover in between.
New research on the Yangtze River Basin has found that these especially brutal “compound” heatwaves follow a hidden rhythm, one that repeats every 10 to 30 days.
The team has now traced exactly how the atmosphere and the ground beneath it conspire to keep the heat going.
The study was led by Yitian Qian from the Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.
Why hot nights matter so much
A heatwave that fades after sunset gives your body, and the land itself, a chance to reset.
Temperatures drop, buildings release the heat they soaked up during the day, and people get at least a few hours where the body isn’t fighting to stay cool.
A heatwave that doesn’t do that is a genuinely different problem. Day-night compound heatwaves, where the heat just persists straight through the night, are dangerous precisely because that recovery window vanishes entirely.
Hospitals tend to see this pattern show up in the data too, since bodies under sustained heat stress with no overnight relief face real cardiovascular strain.
Despite how damaging these events can be, how they actually build over the course of days and weeks has stayed surprisingly murky.
To get at that, the researchers pulled together 64 years of observational and reanalysis data, from 1961 to 2024, comparing daytime-only heatwaves, nighttime-only heatwaves, and the compound kind across China.
One region keeps standing out
A clear pattern emerged pretty quickly. Compound heatwaves cluster heavily over the Yangtze River Basin.
This basin is home to hundreds of millions of people and some of China’s most productive farmland.
Unlike the other two types, compound heatwaves are tied unusually closely to that 10-to-30-day rhythm in the atmosphere.
That suggests there’s a recurring atmospheric cycle quietly setting the stage for these events well before anyone actually feels the heat arrive.
A slow buildup
The team found compound heatwaves unfold in two stages. Roughly a week before one hits, rising air and increased rainfall leave the soil wetter than usual.
On its own, that doesn’t look like much, just some extra rain passing through.
But it turns out to matter enormously for what happens next, almost like the land is unknowingly storing up fuel for the heat that follows.
Damp ground and shifting wind combine
As the heatwave gets closer, an atmospheric wave pattern drifting eastward pushes high-pressure, anticyclonic conditions over the basin.
Clouds thin out, skies clear, and a lot more sunlight starts reaching the ground than usual.
Here’s where the earlier rain comes into play, in the worst way possible.
With the soil already wet, that extra sunlight drives strong evapotranspiration, pumping moisture up off the land and into the lower atmosphere.
Meanwhile, winds from the southwest carry in more warm, damp air from southern China and the surrounding oceans.
Put it together and you get a lower atmosphere that’s both hot and unusually humid – exactly the recipe for scorching days and nights that refuse to cool.
More than daytime heat spilling over
“Compound heatwaves are not simply daytime heat continuing into the night,” Qian said.
“They result from the coordinated evolution of atmospheric circulation, radiation, soil moisture, and moisture transport over a period of several days.”
In other words, these aren’t just regular heatwaves that happen to drag on longer than usual.
They’re their own distinct weather phenomenon, assembled from several interacting pieces, including wind, rain, sunlight, and soil moisture.
Warning signs appear days earlier
Because all of this unfolds days before the heat actually arrives, there’s a genuinely useful implication buried in here.
Shifts in rainfall, soil moisture, and large-scale wind patterns before a heatwave even starts could give forecasters an early signal, a chance to see compound heat extremes coming before they hit.
In future research, the scientists plan to dig further into how both tropical and midlatitude atmospheric variability feed into these events.
They’ll also assess whether these early warning signs can sharpen forecasts enough to give people more time to prepare – before the heat arrives and the nights stop bringing relief.
The study is published in the journal Atmospheric and Oceanic Science Letters.

title: Orange alert in 20 districts for thunderstorms, lightning - The Times of India
search_term: ("heat advisory" OR "heat action plan" OR "heat alert" OR "IMD warning" OR "IMD alert" OR "red alert" OR "orange alert" OR "yellow alert" OR "NDMA advisory" OR "cooling shelter" OR "relief measures" OR "heat compensation" OR "severe weather warning") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
Ranchi: The Met office has issued an orange alert for 20 districts, warning of isolated moderate thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of 30-40 kmph. A yellow alert is in place for the remaining four districts till Thursday.
The orange alert covers Garhwa, Chatra, Palamu, Latehar, Sahibganj, Pakur, Godda, Dumka, Deoghar, Jamtara, Giridih, Hazaribag, Koderma, Ramgarh, Bokaro, Dhanbad, Ranchi, Lohardaga, Gumla and Khunti. Simdega, West Singhbhum, Seraikela-Kharsawan and East Singhbhum remain under a yellow alert.
For Thursday and Friday, the Ranchi weather office has issued an orange warning for 18 districts. These are Hazaribag, Koderma, Ramgarh, Bokaro, Dhanbad, Giridih, Ranchi, Lohardaga, Gumla, Khunti, East Singhbhum, West Singhbhum, Seraikela-Kharsawan, Simdega, Garhwa, Chatra, Palamu and Latehar. Deoghar, Jamtara, Dumka, Pakur, Godda and Sahibganj have been placed under a yellow warning.
“The conditions are favourable for thunder activity. As temperatures rise during the first half of the day and moisture remains available, thunderstorms are likely to form, mainly from the second half of the day till late evening,” said
Abhishek Anand, deputy director of Ranchi Met office.
Anand advised residents, particularly farmers, to take precautions.
IMD said heavy rain was recorded at one location, while isolated parts of the state received light to moderate rain with thunderstorms in the 24 hours till Wednesday morning.
Jama in Dumka recorded the highest rainfall of 65 mm. Baharagora recorded the highest temperature of 37 degrees Celsius, while Netarhat registered the lowest of 20.1°C. Ranchi received 18 mm of rain, with a maximum temperature of 31.1°C and a minimum of 22.8°C.
